related_questions.question: Can you live a normal life with Addisons' disease?
related_questions.snippet: The prognosis for Addison's disease is generally good. Although people who have Addison's disease will need to take medicine for the rest of their lives, they can live normal, healthy lives. The dosages of these medications, however, need to be closely monitored to prevent over- or under-treatment.

related_questions.question: What is the cause of Addison's disease?

text_blocks.snippet: Addison's disease, also known as primary adrenal insufficiency, is primarily caused by damage to the adrenal cortex, leading to insufficient production of hormones like cortisol and aldosterone. The most common cause is an autoimmune reaction where the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the adrenal glands. Other causes include infections like tuberculosis, fungal infections, or HIV, as well as genetic disorders, tumors, or bleeding in the adrenal glands. In rare cases, it can be linked to cancer metastasis or the use of certain medications.
snippet_highlighted_words: damage to the adrenal cortex, leading to insufficient production of hormones like cortisol and aldosterone

list.snippet: This is the most frequent cause of Addison's disease, accounting for a large percentage of cases.
In autoimmune Addison's, the body's immune system mistakenly identifies the adrenal cortex as a threat and attacks it, causing damage and reducing hormone production.
Certain infections can directly damage the adrenal glands, leading to Addison's disease.
Examples include tuberculosis (TB), fungal infections, and HIV, which can weaken the immune system and make it susceptible to adrenal gland damage.
In rare instances, Addison's disease can be inherited due to genetic defects that affect the development or function of the adrenal glands.
Tumors in the adrenal glands can disrupt their function and lead to insufficient hormone production.
Tumors can also be cancerous and metastasize to the adrenal glands from other parts of the body.

list.title: Hemorrhage:
list.snippet: Bleeding into the adrenal glands can also damage them and lead to Addison's disease.

list.title: Medications:
list.snippet: Certain medications, such as some antifungal drugs, can sometimes trigger Addison's disease.

list.title: Surgical Removal:
list.snippet: Surgical removal of the adrenal glands to treat other conditions can also result in Addison's.
It's important to distinguish Addison's disease from secondary adrenal insufficiency, which arises from problems with the pituitary gland (which signals the adrenal glands to produce hormones).
Pituitary tumors, infections, and even traumatic brain injury can affect the pituitary's ability to produce the necessary hormones, leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency.
Sudden cessation of corticosteroid use can also cause secondary adrenal insufficiency.
